The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Three integrations by parts give $|\widehat\varphi(k)|\le\|\varphi\|_1$ for $0\le k\le1$ and $|\widehat\varphi(k)|\le k^{-3}\|\varphi^{(3)}\|_1$ for $k\ge1$. Hence $\int_0^\infty k|\widehat\varphi(k)|\,dk\le\frac12\|\varphi\|_1+\|\varphi^{(3)}\|_1$, so $B$ is a continuous linear functional on each fixed-support test space. Applying the same bound to $\psi(v,\cdot)$ and integrating over the compact $v$-projection bounds $|\langle K,\psi\rangle|$ by a constant times the suprema of $|\psi|$ and $|\partial_s^3\psi|$ on its compact support; thus $K$ is also a distribution and its displayed pairing is absolutely convergent.

If $q=\eta+ix$ with $\eta>0$, an antiderivative of $e^{-qk}$ is $-q^{-1}e^{-qk}$ by [F2]. Applying integration by parts to its real and imaginary parts gives
$$\int_0^R e^{-qk}\,dk=\frac{1-e^{-qR}}q,\qquad \int_0^R ke^{-qk}\,dk=-\frac{R e^{-qR}}q+\frac{1-e^{-qR}}{q^2}.$$
By [F3]–[F4], $|e^{-qR}|=e^{-\eta R}$ and $R e^{-\eta R}\to0$; therefore $\int_0^\infty ke^{-qk}\,dk=q^{-2}$. For $a=x_0+i\eta$, take $q=\eta+i(s-x_0)=i(s-a)$ to obtain
$$-\frac1{(s-a)^2}=\int_0^\infty k e^{-k\operatorname{Im}a}e^{-ik(s-\operatorname{Re}a)}\,dk.$$
In particular this represents every constant positive damping $-(s-i\epsilon)^{-2}$.

Fix a compact parameter set $V$ and a compact interval $[-R,R]$ containing the $s$-support of a test $\psi$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder, obtained by applying [F8] twice, gives
$$d_\epsilon(v,s)=d_{0,\epsilon}(v)+d_{1,\epsilon}(v)s+s^2r_\epsilon(v,s),$$
where $d_{0,\epsilon}=d_\epsilon(v,0)$, $d_{1,\epsilon}=\partial_s d_\epsilon(v,0)$, and $r_\epsilon$ is uniformly bounded on $V\times[-R,R]$. Put $q_\epsilon=1-i\epsilon d_{1,\epsilon}$ and $a_\epsilon=i\epsilon d_{0,\epsilon}/q_\epsilon$. Direct multiplication gives
$$s-i\epsilon d_\epsilon(v,s)=q_\epsilon(s-a_\epsilon)-i\epsilon s^2r_\epsilon.$$
Moreover
$$\operatorname{Im}a_\epsilon=\frac{\epsilon d_{0,\epsilon}}{1+\epsilon^2d_{1,\epsilon}^2}\asymp\epsilon,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a_\epsilon=\frac{-\epsilon^2d_{0,\epsilon}d_{1,\epsilon}}{1+\epsilon^2d_{1,\epsilon}^2}=O(\epsilon^2),$$
uniformly on $V$.

The linearized kernel $-q_\epsilon^{-2}(s-a_\epsilon)^{-2}$ has the representation of step 1.2. Pairing it with $\psi(v,s)$ and using Fubini gives the $v,k$ integrand
$$q_\epsilon(v)^{-2}k e^{-k\operatorname{Im}a_\epsilon(v)}e^{ik\operatorname{Re}a_\epsilon(v)}\widehat\psi(v,k).$$
Three integrations by parts in $s$ show that $k|\widehat\psi(v,k)|$ is integrable over $V\times(0,\infty)$; sigma-finiteness follows from [F7] and [F6] justifies the order change. The integrand converges pointwise to $k\widehat\psi(v,k)$ and is bounded by an integrable constant multiple of it. Dominated convergence [F5] therefore gives the limit $\langle K,\psi\rangle$.

Let $D_\epsilon=s-i\epsilon d_\epsilon(v,s)$ and $L_\epsilon=q_\epsilon(s-a_\epsilon)$. On the compact set, [A1] gives $|D_\epsilon|\ge c'\sqrt{s^2+\epsilon^2}$ and $|D_\epsilon|\le C'\sqrt{s^2+\epsilon^2}$. step 1.3 gives $\operatorname{Im}a_\epsilon\ge c\epsilon$ and $|\operatorname{Re}a_\epsilon|\le C\epsilon^2$. If $|s|\ge2C\epsilon^2$, then $|s-\operatorname{Re}a_\epsilon|\ge|s|/2$; otherwise $|s|=O(\epsilon^2)$ and $|\operatorname{Im}a_\epsilon|\ge c\epsilon$. Thus $|L_\epsilon|\ge c'\sqrt{s^2+\epsilon^2}$ for small $\epsilon$, while the upper bound follows from bounded $q_\epsilon$ and $a_\epsilon=O(\epsilon)$. The factorization in step 1.3 gives $|D_\epsilon-L_\epsilon|\le C'\epsilon s^2$. Therefore
$$|D_\epsilon^{-2}-L_\epsilon^{-2}|=\frac{|D_\epsilon-L_\epsilon|\,|D_\epsilon+L_\epsilon|}{|D_\epsilon|^2|L_\epsilon|^2}\le C'\frac{\epsilon s^2}{(s^2+\epsilon^2)^{3/2}}.$$
The integral of this bound over $|s|\le\epsilon$ is $O(\epsilon)$, and over $\epsilon<|s|\le R$ is $O(\epsilon\log(R/\epsilon))$; both tend to zero. Since $\psi$ is bounded and $V$ has finite measure by [F7], the pairing difference tends to zero.

step 2.2 shows that replacing the variable-damping kernel by the linearized kernel changes every compact-test pairing by a quantity tending to zero; step 2.1 gives the latter's limit as $\langle K,\psi\rangle$. Hence $K_\epsilon\to K=1\otimes B$ in distributions.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. Identify parenthesizations by the isometry fixing
elementary tensors: the product pairing is the same on their dense span,
so the map and its inverse extend to the completions. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $h\in H$, the map $C_h:H\to\mathbb C$, $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$, is linear and bounded:
$|C_h(v)|=|(v,h)_1|\le\|h\|\,\|v\|$ by
[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]].
For any Hilbert space $K$, identify $\mathbb C\widehat\otimes K$ with $K$
by $J_K(z\otimes v)=zv$. Every algebraic tensor is $1\otimes w$;
the tensor norm is then $\|w\|$, so $J_K$ extends to a surjective isometry
on the completion (with inverse $w\mapsto1\otimes w$).
Throughout the following formulas, $C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)}$ means
$J_{H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}}\circ(C_h\widehat\otimes I)$, with
$I$ the identity on $H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}$.
The bounded tensor-map supplier therefore applies and gives norm at most
$\|h\|$. This includes $n=1$, where $H^{\widehat\otimes0}=\mathbb C$.
Contraction commutes with permutations of the remaining $n-1$ factors,
so it takes symmetric or antisymmetric tensors to the corresponding
$(n-1)$-particle sector (and to $\mathbb C$ for $n=1$).

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h$ is the bounded functional above, its tensor extension is supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the
whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ be a separable
complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and let $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ be its bosonic Fock space and finite-particle domain.
For $h\in H$ define on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ the Segal field
$$\phi_0(h):=2^{-1/2}\bigl(a^\dagger(h)+a(h)\bigr).$$
For $h\ne0$, this symmetric operator is essentially self-adjoint; write
$\Phi(h)=\overline{\phi_0(h)}$. If $r=\|h\|$, $e=h/r$, $K=e^\perp$,
$G=\mathcal F_s(K)$, choose a countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $G$
whose vectors are finite-particle, and use the one-mode splitting of
[[lem-qft-fock-one-mode-splitting]] followed by the Hermite unitary
$|n\rangle\mapsto g_n$ into $L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C)$ with pairing
$\langle f,g\rangle_2=\int\overline f g$ to write a vector as
$(f_j)_{j\in J}\in\ell^2(J;L^2(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C))$. Then the exact domain and
action are
$$D(\Phi(h))=\left\{(f_j):\sum_{j\in J}\int_{\mathbb R}(1+r^2x^2)|f_j(x)|^2\,dx<\infty\right\},\qquad (\Phi(h)f)_j(x)=rx f_j(x).$$
For $h=0$, $\phi_0(0)$ closes to the zero operator on all of $\mathcal F_s(H)$.

Define $\epsilon(z)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}z^{\otimes n}/\sqrt{n!}$ for $z\in H$.
There are unitaries $W(h)$ determined on these total exponential vectors by
$$W(h)\epsilon(z)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|h\|^2}{4} +\frac{i}{\sqrt2}\langle h,z\rangle_2\right) \epsilon\!\left(z+\frac{i h}{\sqrt2}\right).$$
They obey
$$W(h)W(k)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i}{2}\operatorname{Im}\langle h,k\rangle_2\right)W(h+k),\qquad \langle\Omega,W(h)\Omega\rangle_2=e^{-\|h\|^2/4},$$
and $h\mapsto W(h)$ is strongly continuous. For every $h$, the one-parameter
group $t\mapsto W(th)$ has norm derivative at zero exactly on
$D(\Phi(h))$, with derivative $i\Phi(h)$ (for $h=0$ this is the zero
generator). Thus the displayed bounded Weyl operators have precisely the
closed Segal fields as their generators; no point-field or measurement claim
is included.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

$$\exp:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(0,\infty)$$
is a bijection.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Assume Countable Choice and use Euclidean Lebesgue measure. Let $m\ge0$. For $m=0$ take $\mathbb R^0$ to be a singleton with measure $1$. For each sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$ let $d_\epsilon:\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth and real-valued. Assume that for every compact $V\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ and every $R>0$ there are constants $c,C,M,\epsilon_0>0$ such that, on $V\times[-R,R]$ and for $0<\epsilon<\epsilon_0$,
$$c\le d_\epsilon(v,s)\le C,\qquad |\partial_s d_\epsilon(v,s)|+|\partial_s^2d_\epsilon(v,s)|\le M.$$
For $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ set $\widehat\varphi(k)=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(s)e^{-iks}\,ds$ and define $B$ by
$$\langle B,\varphi\rangle:=\int_0^\infty k\widehat\varphi(k)\,dk.$$
For $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ write $\widehat\psi(v,k)=\int_{\mathbb R}\psi(v,s)e^{-iks}\,ds$ and define $K$ by
$$\langle K,\psi\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^m}\int_0^\infty k\widehat\psi(v,k)\,dk\,dv.$$
Then $B$ and $K$ are distributions, $B$ is the lower boundary denoted $-(s-i0)^{-2}$, and $K=1\otimes B$ in the explicitly defined pairing above. The smooth kernels
$$K_\epsilon(v,s):=-\bigl(s-i\epsilon d_\epsilon(v,s)\bigr)^{-2}$$
converge to $K$ in the distributional sense: $\int K_\epsilon(v,s)\psi(v,s)\,dv\,ds\to\langle K,\psi\rangle$ for every such $\psi$. When $s$ and $\epsilon$ carry units of length, $d_\epsilon$ is dimensionless.

derivations.claim: By [F4], $\mathcal H$ is a complex Hilbert space; the change from its first-variable-linear inner product to $\langle h,q\rangle_2=\int\bar hq$ is conjugation and preserves its norm. Let $D$ be the countable dense rational box-step family in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ from [F5]. Restricting $D$ to $(0,\infty)$ is countable. For any $h\in\mathcal H$, extend $h$ by zero to $\tilde h\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ and approximate $\tilde h$ by $d\in D$; then $\|h-d|_{(0,\infty)}\|_2\le\|\tilde h-d\|_2$. Thus $\mathcal H$ is separable and [F3] applies.

Fix $f$ supported in a compact interval $K$ and write $F_f(k)=\int_K f(U)e^{ikU}\,dU$. For $0<k\le1$, $|F_f(k)|\le\|f\|_1$. For $k\ge1$, two integrations by parts with vanishing endpoint terms give $|F_f(k)|\le k^{-2}\|f''\|_1$. Therefore
$$\|h_f\|_2^2=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\infty k|F_f(k)|^2\,dk\le\frac{\|f\|_1^2+\|f''\|_1^2}{8\pi}<\infty.$$
The same estimate holds for $\bar f$; on fixed $K$, each $L^1$ norm is bounded by $|K|$ times the corresponding supremum seminorm. This proves both membership in $\mathcal H$ and continuity on each fixed-support test space.

Since $f\mapsto h_f$ is linear, $f\mapsto h_{\bar f}$ is conjugate-linear, annihilation is conjugate-linear in its one-particle argument, and creation is linear, $J$ is linear. Its two summands preserve the finite-particle domain by [F1]–[F2]. For fixed finite-particle vectors $\Psi,\Xi$, only finitely many sectors occur; Cauchy--Schwarz [F11] and the sector bounds [F2] bound $|\langle\Psi,J(f)\Xi\rangle_2|$ by a finite constant depending on $\Psi,\Xi$ times $\|h_f\|_2+\|h_{\bar f}\|_2$; hence each matrix coefficient is a continuous test distribution. If $f$ is real, $J(f)=a(h_f)+a^\dagger(h_f)=\sqrt2\,\phi_0(h_f)$, so [F3] gives $\overline{J(f)}=\sqrt2\Phi(h_f)$. Finally $J(g)\Omega=a^\dagger(h_g)\Omega$, and the sector formulas in [F1] give
$$\langle\Omega,J(\bar f)J(g)\Omega\rangle_2=\langle h_f,h_g\rangle_2.$$
In particular the form at $g=f$ is $\|h_f\|_2^2\ge0$.

For $\epsilon>0$ and real $s$, direct integration with $\operatorname{Re}(\epsilon+is)>0$ gives
$$C_\epsilon(s):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\infty k e^{-\epsilon k}e^{-iks}\,dk=-\frac1{4\pi(s-i\epsilon)^2}.$$
For $f,g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$, $\varphi_{f,g}(s)=\int_{\mathbb R}\overline{f(x+s)}g(x)\,dx$ is a compact smooth test, and Fubini [F8] gives $\widehat\varphi_{f,g}(k)=\overline{F_f(k)}F_g(k)$. Hence
$$\langle C_\epsilon,\varphi_{f,g}\rangle=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\infty k e^{-\epsilon k}\overline{F_f(k)}F_g(k)\,dk,$$
the damped vacuum covariance of step 2.1. For a general test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$, its Fourier transform $\widehat\varphi(k)=\int\varphi(s)e^{-iks}\,ds$ satisfies $|\widehat\varphi(k)|\le k^{-3}\|\varphi^{(3)}\|_1$ for $k\ge1$ by [F6]. Thus $k|\widehat\varphi(k)|$ is integrable on $(0,\infty)$, and [F7] shows $\langle C_\epsilon,\varphi\rangle\to(4\pi)^{-1}\int_0^\infty k\widehat\varphi(k)\,dk$. This defines the boundary distribution $C(s)=-(4\pi)^{-1}(s-i0)^{-2}$ and, by the same domination on $\varphi_{f,g}$, its pairing is exactly the covariance in step 2.1.

By [F9], $U_\kappa$ is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism onto $(-\infty,0)$. If $g$ is supported in $[a,b]$, then $f_g$ is supported in the compact interval $[U_\kappa(a),U_\kappa(b)]\subset(-\infty,0)$, separated from $0$; its zero extension is smooth. The chain rule on this compact interval bounds every fixed-support derivative seminorm of $f_g$ by finitely many such seminorms of $g$, so [F1]–[F2] show $j_\kappa(g)=J(f_g)$ is well-defined and continuous. In the two-point test pairing the smooth change of variable contributes $U_\kappa'(u)U_\kappa'(u')$, where $U_\kappa'(u)=e^{-\kappa u}$. Put $v=(u+u')/2$, $s=u-u'$, and $b=\kappa/2$. Direct algebra gives
$$U_\kappa(u)-U_\kappa(u')=b^{-1}e^{-\kappa v}\sinh(bs),\qquad U_\kappa'(u)U_\kappa'(u')=e^{-2\kappa v}.$$
Applying [F10] to the damped kernel $C_\epsilon(U_\kappa(u)-U_\kappa(u'))U_\kappa'(u)U_\kappa'(u')$ yields
$$-\frac1{4\pi}\left(Y_b(s)-i\epsilon e^{\kappa v}\right)^{-2},\qquad Y_b(s)=\frac{\sinh(bs)}b.$$
The linear change $(u,u')\mapsto(v,s)$ has determinant $-1$, hence absolute Jacobian $1$. Now change variables $y=Y_b(s)$, which is the smooth increasing diffeomorphism defined in the Statement. In each test pairing this replaces $\psi(v,s)$ by the compact smooth test $\widetilde\psi(v,y)=\psi(v,Y_b^{-1}(y))(Y_b^{-1})'(y)$. The positive smooth damping $e^{\kappa v}$ is bounded above and below on each compact test support, so [F12] in the $y$-coordinate gives the boundary $-(4\pi)^{-1}Y_b^*((y-i0)^{-2})$. Since $b=\kappa/2$, this is exactly $C_\kappa(s)$ as defined in the Statement. For $0<\epsilon<\beta/2$, the analytic regularization satisfies
$$\frac{\sinh(b(s-i\epsilon))}{b}=\cos(b\epsilon)\left(Y_b(s)-i\epsilon d_\epsilon(s)\right),\qquad d_\epsilon(s)=\frac{\cosh(bs)\tan(b\epsilon)}{b\epsilon}.$$
After the change of variable $y=Y_b(s)$, the damping is $\widetilde d_\epsilon(y)=d_\epsilon(Y_b^{-1}(y))$. On every compact support this family is smooth, bounded above and below positively, and converges smoothly to $\cosh(bY_b^{-1}(y))>0$, so it meets [F12] with $m=0$. Thus [F12] gives the same boundary for $\sinh(b(s-i\epsilon))^{-2}$; the scalar factor $\cos(b\epsilon)^{-2}$ tends to $1$. This identifies $C_\kappa$ with the lower boundary of $-\kappa^2(16\pi)^{-1}\operatorname{csch}^2(bz)$.

The notation $i0$ in the Statement is therefore the lower-half-plane boundary induced by the positive orientation $U_\kappa'(u)>0$; it is a distributional two-point covariance, not an ordinary value at $s=0$. The construction uses only smooth compact tests in one coordinate and makes no four-dimensional null pullback.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2((0,\infty),dk;\mathbb C),\qquad \langle h,q\rangle_2=\int_0^\infty\overline{h(k)}q(k)\,dk,$$
using the second-variable-linear convention. For
$f\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ define
$$h_f(k)=\sqrt{\frac{k}{4\pi}}\int_{\mathbb R}f(U)e^{ikU}\,dU\quad(k>0).$$
Then $h_f,h_{\bar f}\in\mathcal H$, and $f\mapsto h_f$ is continuous on each fixed-compact-support test space. With the bosonic Fock conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], define on its finite-particle domain
$$J(f)=a(h_{\bar f})+a^\dagger(h_f).$$
This is a complex-linear operator-valued distribution on that invariant domain. For real $f$, its closure is $\overline{J(f)}=\sqrt2\,\Phi(h_f)$, where $\Phi(h_f)$ is the closed Segal field of [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]; the corresponding Weyl one-parameter group has generator $i\Phi(h_f)$. The vacuum two-point form is positive type and has boundary kernel
$$C(s)=-\frac{1}{4\pi(s-i0)^2},$$
where $s-i0$ means the distributional limit from $s-i\epsilon$, $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

For $\kappa>0$ with units of inverse length, let $u,U$ have units of length and set
$$U_\kappa(u)=-\kappa^{-1}e^{-\kappa u},\qquad u_\kappa(U)=-\kappa^{-1}\log(-\kappa U)\quad(U<0).$$
For $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ put $f_g(U)=g(u_\kappa(U))$ for $U<0$ and $f_g(U)=0$ for $U\ge0$, and define $j_\kappa(g)=J(f_g)$. The zero extension is smooth and compactly supported. Its vacuum covariance is the positive-type distribution
$$C_\kappa(s)=-\frac{\kappa^2}{16\pi}\,\operatorname{csch}^2\!\left(\frac{\kappa}{2}(s-i0)\right).$$
Here the notation is fixed as follows: for $b=\kappa/2$, set $Y_b(s)=\sinh(bs)/b$. Since $Y_b'(s)=\cosh(bs)>0$ and $Y_b(s)\to\pm\infty$ as $s\to\pm\infty$, it is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism. Define $\operatorname{csch}^2(b(s-i0)):=b^{-2}Y_b^*((y-i0)^{-2})$, where
$$\langle Y_b^*T,\varphi\rangle:=\left\langle T,\varphi(Y_b^{-1}(y))(Y_b^{-1})'(y)\right\rangle.$$
This is a one-dimensional chiral test-coordinate model. It asserts no restriction of a four-dimensional field to a null curve.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

For the seminorms of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]], a basic neighbourhood of $f_0\in\mathcal S$ is
$$\{f:p_{\alpha_r\beta_r}(f-f_0)<\varepsilon_r\ (1\le r\le m)\},\qquad m<\infty,\quad\varepsilon_r>0.$$
The empty intersection is the whole space. The topology consists of unions of these neighbourhoods. A sequence $f_k$ converges to $f$ precisely when $p_{\alpha\beta}(f_k-f)\to0$ for every pair of multi-indices: necessity follows from the one-condition neighbourhoods, and sufficiency follows by taking the maximum of the finitely many convergence thresholds in a basic neighbourhood.

A complex topological vector space is called locally convex here when zero has a base of convex balanced sets; balanced means $|c|\le1$ implies $cV\subseteq V$. The displayed sets about zero are convex and balanced by the seminorm inequalities. They also show addition is continuous, by halving each tolerance. Scalar multiplication is jointly continuous: near $(c_0,f_0)$, restrict $|c-c_0|<1$ and use
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(cf-c_0f_0)\le (|c_0|+1)p_{\alpha\beta}(f-f_0)+|c-c_0|p_{\alpha\beta}(f_0).$$
There are finitely many bounds to enforce. Finally $p_{00}(f-g)>0$ for distinct functions; balls of radius less than half this number separate them. Thus this is a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space. All these verifications use only finite choices.

Fix an integer $n\geq1$.  A **tempered distribution** on $\mathbb R^n$ is a
continuous complex-linear functional

$$u:\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow\mathbb C,$$

where Schwartz space and its locally convex topology are those of
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]] and
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]].  The space of all such functionals
is denoted $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.

We write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$.  This pairing is bilinear:
the test variable is not conjugated.  Thus $u(a\varphi+b\psi)=
a\langle u,\varphi\rangle+b\langle u,\psi\rangle$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C$.
The zero functional is tempered.  Continuity is topological continuity, and,
because the Schwartz topology is generated by a countable cofinal family of
seminorms, it is equivalently continuity on every convergent sequence.  No
choice principle is used in this definition.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be
holomorphic, and let $\gamma:[0,1]\to\Omega$ be a closed rectifiable contour. If
$\gamma$ is path-homotopic relative to the endpoints to a constant loop in
$\Omega$, then

$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=0.$$

Let $\gamma=x+iy:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be a rectifiable contour in the sense of [[def-complex-contours-reversal-concatenation-and-closedness]] and let $f=u+iv$ be continuous on its trace, with real and imaginary parts from [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Define
$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz:=\int_a^b u(\gamma(t))\,dx(t)-\int_a^b v(\gamma(t))\,dy(t)+i\left(\int_a^b v(\gamma(t))\,dx(t)+\int_a^b u(\gamma(t))\,dy(t)\right),$$
where the four integrals are the real Riemann–Stieltjes integrals of [[def-riemann-stieltjes-sum-and-integral]]. Their existence is proved in [[thm-existence-of-complex-line-integrals-on-rectifiable-paths]]. On a singleton parameter interval the integral is $0$.

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ be rectifiable and let $f$ be continuous on its trace. Then the complex line integral [[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]] and the absolute line integral [[def-absolute-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]] both exist.

Let $F$ be a primitive of a continuous function $f$ on an open set containing the trace of a rectifiable contour $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$. If $F'=f$ is continuous, then
$$\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=F(\gamma(b))-F(\gamma(a)).$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

$$\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z,$$
and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$. The function $f$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** if the limit

$$ \lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\ne0,\ a+h\in U}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$

exists in the metric of [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. Its value is the **complex derivative** of $f$ at $a$, denoted $f'(a)$. The increments are nonzero and remain in the domain; because $U$ is open, all sufficiently small increments are allowed.

The function $f$ is **holomorphic on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. The word analytic is reserved for the local power-series notion.

Let $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ have radius $R$. If $|z-a|<R$, then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z$ and
$$f'(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}n c_n(z-a)^{n-1}.$$
Consequently $f$ is holomorphic on its open disc of convergence ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
Write $\sinh w=(e^w-e^{-w})/2$ and $\operatorname{csch}w=1/\sinh w$ where the denominator is nonzero. From [F5]–[F6], $\sinh(w+i\pi)=-\sinh w$, $\sinh(-w)=-\sinh(w)$, and $\sinh w=0$ exactly when $w\in i\pi\mathbb Z$. Thus $C(z)$ has poles only at $z=in\beta$ ($n\in\mathbb Z$). It is holomorphic on the stated strip: $\sinh$ is holomorphic by [F5] and the chain rule; where it is nonzero, its reciprocal is complex differentiable because
$$\frac{1/\sinh(w+h)-1/\sinh(w)}{h}=-\frac{\sinh(w+h)-\sinh(w)}{h\sinh(w+h)\sinh(w)}$$
converges as $h\to0$, using continuity from [F7]. The exponential addition law gives period $i\beta$, and oddness of $\sinh$ gives evenness of $C$. These are identities of the general analytic kernel; their distributional boundary interpretation follows once the boundary has been constructed.

Set $z_0=-i\beta$ and $\delta=z-z_0$. Since $bz_0=-i\pi$, $\sinh(bz)=-b\delta q(\delta)$, where $q(\delta)=\sinh(b\delta)/(b\delta)$ for $\delta\ne0$ and $q(0)=1$. Its power series $q(\delta)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}(b\delta)^{2m}/(2m+1)!$ converges for all $\delta$ as a subseries of the complex exponential series. The termwise-differentiation theorem in [F7] makes $q$ holomorphic and its displayed series makes it even. Since $q(0)=1$, continuity from [F7] makes $q$ nonzero on a small disk; the reciprocal difference quotient using [F7] makes $q^{-2}$ holomorphic there, and its even series is $1+O(\delta^2)$. Therefore
$$C(z)=-\frac{L}{(z-z_0)^2}+H(z),\qquad L=\frac{A}{b^2},$$
where $H(z)$ is holomorphic at $z_0$, with no simple-pole term.

Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ and $0<\epsilon<\beta$. Integrate $e^{-i\omega z}C(z)$ around the clockwise rectangle with top from $-R-i\epsilon$ to $R-i\epsilon$ and bottom at imaginary part $-(\beta+\epsilon)$. Its interior lies in $-2\beta<\operatorname{Im}z<0$ and contains only $z_0$. The holomorphic part $e^{-i\omega z}H(z)$ integrates to zero by [F3] on a slightly enlarged convex rectangle: its closure contains the contour, and convexity contracts the closed contour to a constant loop inside that open domain. For the double-pole term, the function $(e^{-i\omega z}-e^{-i\omega z_0})/(z-z_0)$ extends holomorphically at $z_0$, so [F3] gives zero for its contour integral. To evaluate the remaining simple pole, write $a=\beta-\epsilon>0$ and $c=\epsilon>0$. Relative to $z_0$, the rectangle's vertices are $(-R,a),(R,a),(R,-c),(-R,-c)$. With $\theta_a=\arctan(a/R)$ and $\theta_c=\arctan(c/R)$, the continuous argument changes along its four clockwise sides by $-\pi+2\theta_a$, $-\theta_a-\theta_c$, $-\pi+2\theta_c$, and $-\theta_a-\theta_c$, respectively; their sum is $-2\pi$. The net change of $\log|z-z_0|$ is zero, so $\oint dz/(z-z_0)=-2\pi i$ and $\oint e^{-i\omega z}(z-z_0)^{-1}dz=-2\pi i e^{-i\omega z_0}$. The function $e^{-i\omega z}/(z-z_0)$ is single-valued and has continuous derivative on a neighborhood of the contour, which avoids $z_0$; by [F4] its derivative integrates to zero. Since
$$d\!\left(\frac{e^{-i\omega z}}{z-z_0}\right)=\left(-i\omega\frac{e^{-i\omega z}}{z-z_0}-\frac{e^{-i\omega z}}{(z-z_0)^2}\right)dz,$$
we obtain $\oint e^{-i\omega z}(z-z_0)^{-2}dz=-2\pi\omega e^{-i\omega z_0}$.

The vertical-side integrals tend to zero as $R\to\infty$: for $\operatorname{Re}z=R$, $\operatorname{csch}^2(bz)=4e^{-2bz}(1-e^{-2bz})^{-2}=O(e^{-2bR})$ uniformly on the finite vertical interval, and the analogous formula with $e^{2bz}$ gives the same bound on $\operatorname{Re}z=-R$. The factor $e^{-i\omega z}$ is bounded there for fixed $\omega,\epsilon$. The bottom line is the top line translated by $-i\beta$; periodicity of $C$ and the Fourier phase multiply its oriented integral by $-e^{-\beta\omega}$. Combining this with step 2.1 gives
$$ (1-e^{-\beta\omega})I_\epsilon(\omega)=2\pi L\omega e^{-\beta\omega},$$
where $I_\epsilon(\omega)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-i\omega(s-i\epsilon)}C(s-i\epsilon)\,ds$.

For each fixed $0<\epsilon<\beta$, $s\mapsto C(s-i\epsilon)$ has no real pole, is bounded on compact intervals, and decays exponentially at both ends, so it is in $L^1(\mathbb R)$. If $\omega_n\to\omega$, the integrands converge pointwise and are bounded by $|C(s-i\epsilon)|\in L^1$; [F8] therefore makes its Fourier transform $J_\epsilon(\omega)=\int e^{-i\omega s}C(s-i\epsilon)ds$ continuous. Since $I_\epsilon=e^{-\omega\epsilon}J_\epsilon$, step 3.1 yields, for $\omega\ne0$,
$$J_\epsilon(\omega)=2\pi L e^{\omega\epsilon}\frac{\omega}{e^{\beta\omega}-1}.$$
Continuity forces the value at $\omega=0$ to be $2\pi L/\beta$; no point value at zero is left arbitrary.

Define $S(\omega)=2\pi L\omega/(e^{\beta\omega}-1)$ with its continuous value $2\pi L/\beta$ at zero. Continuity bounds $S$ on $[-1,1]$. For $\omega\ge1$, $|S(\omega)|\le C\omega e^{-\beta\omega}$, while for $\omega\le-1$, $|S(\omega)|\le C|\omega|$ because $1-e^{\beta\omega}\ge1-e^{-\beta}$. Thus $|S(\omega)|\le C(1+|\omega|)$ globally. For any Schwartz test $\varphi$, with seminorms $p_{m,n}(\varphi)=\sup_\omega|\omega^m\varphi^{(n)}(\omega)|$, split at $|\omega|=1$: the integral of $(1+|\omega|)|\varphi(\omega)|$ is bounded by a constant times $p_{0,0}(\varphi)+p_{3,0}(\varphi)$, since the tail is bounded by $2p_{3,0}|\omega|^{-2}$. Hence $S$ defines a tempered distribution. For $0<\epsilon\le\beta/2$, $e^{\omega\epsilon}S(\omega)$ is bounded by $C(1+|\omega|)$ for $\omega\le0$ and by $C(1+\omega)e^{-\beta\omega/2}$ for $\omega\ge0$. These bounds make the Schwartz-test product integrable and give an integrable majorant independent of $\epsilon$; [F8] yields $J_\epsilon\to S$ in the tempered-distribution sense. To construct the boundary without assuming a chiral specialization, apply Fourier inversion [F2] to a Schwartz test $\varphi$ and use $C_\epsilon\in L^1$ and $\widehat\varphi\in L^1$ to justify Fubini [F9]:
$$\langle C_\epsilon,\varphi\rangle=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}J_\epsilon(\omega)\widehat\varphi(-\omega)\,d\omega.$$
The same majorant and [F8] give the limit
$$\langle C_{A,b},\varphi\rangle:=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}S(\omega)\widehat\varphi(-\omega)\,d\omega.$$
This is continuous in the Schwartz topology by the seminorm bound above and continuity of the Schwartz Fourier map in [F2]; hence it defines a tempered distribution and $C_\epsilon\to C_{A,b}$ on every Schwartz test. Angular Fourier inversion gives $\widehat{\widehat\varphi}(-\omega)=2\pi\varphi(\omega)$, so the displayed formula applied to $\widehat\varphi$ yields $\langle\widehat C_{A,b},\varphi\rangle=\int S(\omega)\varphi(\omega)d\omega$. Thus the general boundary has exactly the stated spectrum.

For $\omega>0$, the numerator and denominator of $S_{A,b}(\omega)$ are positive; for $\omega<0$ both are negative, and its zero limit $2\pi L/\beta=2A/b$ is positive. Direct algebra gives $S_{A,b}(-\omega)=e^{\beta\omega}S_{A,b}(\omega)$. The analytic period and reflection from step 1.1 give $C(s-i\beta+i\epsilon)=C(s+i\epsilon)=C(-s-i\epsilon)$; reflection preserves Schwartz tests, so step 5.1 gives the stated tested boundary relation. For the chiral specialization $A=\kappa^2/(16\pi)$, $b=\kappa/2$, [F1] identifies the same analytic regularizations with the compact-test boundary $C_\kappa$. Uniqueness of their distributional limit makes it the restriction of $C_{A,b}$, giving its tempered extension. Substituting $L=1/(4\pi)$ and $\beta=2\pi/\kappa$ yields the original chiral spectrum, zero value and ratio. The units follow because the phase $\omega s$ is dimensionless and Fourier transformation integrates once in the coordinate. These are two-point mathematical deductions only; neither the contour proof nor the strip identity establishes a full $C^*$-algebra KMS state or an exact detector transition probability.

Assume Countable Choice. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2((0,\infty),dk;\mathbb C),\qquad \langle h,q\rangle_2=\int_0^\infty\overline{h(k)}q(k)\,dk,$$
using the second-variable-linear convention. For
$f\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ define
$$h_f(k)=\sqrt{\frac{k}{4\pi}}\int_{\mathbb R}f(U)e^{ikU}\,dU\quad(k>0).$$
Then $h_f,h_{\bar f}\in\mathcal H$, and $f\mapsto h_f$ is continuous on each fixed-compact-support test space. With the bosonic Fock conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], define on its finite-particle domain
$$J(f)=a(h_{\bar f})+a^\dagger(h_f).$$
This is a complex-linear operator-valued distribution on that invariant domain. For real $f$, its closure is $\overline{J(f)}=\sqrt2\,\Phi(h_f)$, where $\Phi(h_f)$ is the closed Segal field of [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]; the corresponding Weyl one-parameter group has generator $i\Phi(h_f)$. The vacuum two-point form is positive type and has boundary kernel
$$C(s)=-\frac{1}{4\pi(s-i0)^2},$$
where $s-i0$ means the distributional limit from $s-i\epsilon$, $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

For $\kappa>0$ with units of inverse length, let $u,U$ have units of length and set
$$U_\kappa(u)=-\kappa^{-1}e^{-\kappa u},\qquad u_\kappa(U)=-\kappa^{-1}\log(-\kappa U)\quad(U<0).$$
For $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ put $f_g(U)=g(u_\kappa(U))$ for $U<0$ and $f_g(U)=0$ for $U\ge0$, and define $j_\kappa(g)=J(f_g)$. The zero extension is smooth and compactly supported. Its vacuum covariance is the positive-type distribution
$$C_\kappa(s)=-\frac{\kappa^2}{16\pi}\,\operatorname{csch}^2\!\left(\frac{\kappa}{2}(s-i0)\right).$$
Here the notation is fixed as follows: for $b=\kappa/2$, set $Y_b(s)=\sinh(bs)/b$. Since $Y_b'(s)=\cosh(bs)>0$ and $Y_b(s)\to\pm\infty$ as $s\to\pm\infty$, it is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism. Define $\operatorname{csch}^2(b(s-i0)):=b^{-2}Y_b^*((y-i0)^{-2})$, where
$$\langle Y_b^*T,\varphi\rangle:=\left\langle T,\varphi(Y_b^{-1}(y))(Y_b^{-1})'(y)\right\rangle.$$
This is a one-dimensional chiral test-coordinate model. It asserts no restriction of a four-dimensional field to a null curve.

In particular, for $\kappa>0$ in inverse length, take $A=\kappa^2/(16\pi)$ and $b=\kappa/2$. Then $L=1/(4\pi)$, $\beta=2\pi/\kappa$, and $C_{A,b}$ is precisely the tested chiral covariance $C_\kappa$ of [[lem-tgr-exponential-current]]. Its spectrum and detailed balance are
$$S_\kappa(\omega)=\frac{\omega}{2(e^{2\pi\omega/\kappa}-1)},\qquad S_\kappa(0)=\frac{\kappa}{4\pi},\qquad S_\kappa(-\omega)=e^{2\pi\omega/\kappa}S_\kappa(\omega)\quad(\omega>0).$$
Here $C_\kappa$ has units of inverse length squared and $S_\kappa$ inverse length. This is a two-point strip and detailed-balance statement, including the specified chiral current as a specialization. It does not assert a norm-continuous $C^*$-algebra KMS dynamics or an exact detector transition probability.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Under [A1], change the length-flow coordinate to $u'=u/b$ and define the primed smeared current by $j'(g')=j_\kappa(g'(\cdot/b))$ for $g'\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$. Since $u=bu'$, the current density transforms as $j'(u')=b j_\kappa(bu')$ in the distributional sense, so its two-point covariance is $C'(s')=b^2 C_\kappa(bs')$. Substituting [F1] and using $b>0$ to preserve the lower-boundary orientation gives $C'(s')=C_{b\kappa}(s')$.

Put $\kappa'=b\kappa$ and $\omega'=b\omega$. Then [F2] gives
$$S_{\kappa'}(\omega')=\frac{b\omega}{2(e^{2\pi b\omega/(b\kappa)}-1)}=bS_\kappa(\omega),$$
and therefore $S_{\kappa'}(-\omega')/S_{\kappa'}(\omega')=e^{2\pi\omega/\kappa}$. The phase is preserved exactly when its generator parameter rescales as $E'=bE$, because $E'u'/\sigma=(bE)(u/b)/\sigma=Eu/\sigma$. Equivalently, the length-flow strip width $\beta_\ell=2\pi/\kappa$ rescales to $\beta_\ell'=\beta_\ell/b$, while $\beta_\ell'\omega'=\beta_\ell\omega$.
